key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the scuffle had taken place on the spur of the moment and a sudden fight had taken place in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and there was no pre-meditation or intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses' credibility by noting that the evidence on record indicated the scuffle occurred spontaneously and that there was no intention to kill, supporting the conclusion that the conviction should be modified from Section 304 Part-I to Section 304 Part-II IPC.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: Not stated; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: 08.02.2019 and 01.03.2019; Supreme Court decision: September 21, 2021
legal_representation: Bharat Sood, P. S. Sudheer, Advs. for the Appellant; Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Ms. Mandakini Singh, Karanvir Gogia, Ms. Shivangi Singhal, Ms. Ashima Mandla, Advs. for the Respondent
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Sections 302/34 and 201 IPC; High Court: Modified conviction to Section 304 Part-I/34 IPC and maintained conviction under Section 201 IPC; Supreme Court: Modified conviction to Section 304 Part-II/34 IPC and maintained conviction under Section 201 IPC
prosecution_argument: The State of Punjab argued that the High Court's conviction of the appellant under Section 304 Part-I IPC was incorrect and that there were no grounds to interfere with the High Court's judgment. The State also contended that the case law relied on by the appellant was distinguishable on facts and could not be applied to the case at hand.
defence_argument: The appellant's counsel argued that there was no intention to kill the deceased, the scuffle was a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and it was not a pre-meditated act. They submitted that the conviction under Section 304 Part-I IPC should be modified to Section 304 Part-II IPC, citing the precedent of Uday Singh v. State of U.P. and Shahajan Ali & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that if there was no intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, the conviction under Section 304 Part-I IPC should be modified to Section 304 Part-II IPC.
precedent_relied_upon: Uday Singh v. State of U.P. (2002) 7 SCC 79; Shahajan Ali & Ors. etc. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors. etc. (2017) 11 SC 807
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the Supreme Court found that the scuffle was a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, there was no pre-meditation, and no intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death. Therefore, the conviction under Section 304 Part-I IPC was modified to Section 304 Part-II IPC, while maintaining the conviction under Section 201 IPC.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of seven years and a fine of Rs.10,000/- was imposed. Additionally, the conviction under Section 201 IPC and a sentence of three years’ rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.500/- were maintained.
